passage:
Day one: at the school gate in Ranchi, Ojas, four, clenched both fists and stamped when his mother Trisha said no to the toy stall. She knelt. "Your hands look angry. Want to tell me?" He shouted "Toy!" and she said, "You're frustrated."
Day three: Ojas's fists tightened when his block tower fell. Trisha handed him a soft ball and he squeezed it hard.
Day six: he held up his fists and said, "Angry hands, Amma!" then squeezed the ball.

qa.q: What did Ojas shout when his mother said no to the toy stall?
qa.a: He shouted "Toy!"

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when his fists tightened on day three?
qa.a: He was frustrated or angry that his tower fell, and squeezing the soft ball gave that feeling somewhere to go. He might also have been disappointed after all his careful stacking.

qa.q: What worked well in how Trisha helped Ojas across the days?
qa.a: She gave him words for the feeling and a safe outlet, the soft ball, so that by day six he named it himself.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel on day six when Ojas says, "Angry hands, Amma!"?
qa.a: Trisha is probably pleased and proud that Ojas can now name his feeling and reach for the ball himself.

grounding: A preschooler clenches his fists in anger, and adults offer words for the feeling and a safe outlet such as a soft ball.

passage: The generator had stopped mid-lesson at the tuition class in Nashik, and the room was hot and dim. Ankita, five, was struggling to tie her shoelace, her tongue between her teeth. It slipped again. Her fists clenched and her face went red. Her teacher Jyoti crouched beside her. "Those are strong fists. That knot is being stubborn." She handed Ankita a squishy ball from the shelf. Ankita squeezed it twice, breathed out, and tried the lace again.

qa.q: What was Ankita trying to tie?
qa.a: She was trying to tie her shoelace.

qa.q: What does Ankita's clenched fists and red face suggest she felt, and what else might have added to it?
qa.a: They suggest anger and frustration at the slipping lace. The hot, dim room may have made her feel worse.

qa.q: What could Jyoti try when Ankita gets frustrated again?
qa.a: She can keep offering a squishy ball or another safe outlet and use words such as "stubborn" for the knot.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel when Jyoti calls the knot stubborn?
qa.a: She may feel that her teacher is on her side, and the problem is the knot, not her.

grounding: A preschooler clenches her fists in frustration, and a teacher offers words and a safe outlet.

passage: On the rooftop in Ahmedabad, Harsha's green kite was cut by a neighbour's string and drifted away over the tanks. Harsha's hands curled into tight fists. She stamped, face red. Vikas, her father, put down the spool. “You're angry. That was your best kite.” “I want to hit him!” “Hitting's not okay. But you can squeeze.” He handed her the soft rubber ball from his pocket. Harsha squeezed it hard, again and again. Slowly her fingers loosened, and she asked, “Can we fly the yellow one?”

qa.q: What colour was Harsha's kite that was cut?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What do Harsha's tight fists suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest she was angry and frustrated about losing her best kite. She may also have felt sad under the anger.

qa.q: What did Vikas give Harsha, and why did it help?
qa.a: He gave her a soft rubber ball to squeeze, a safe outlet for her anger along with words for her feeling.

qa.q: How might the neighbour flying the other kite see it?
qa.a: The neighbour might see the cut as part of the kite game, not knowing how upset Harsha felt.

grounding: A child clenches her fists in anger after her kite is cut, and her father offers words and a safe outlet.

passage:
“Ammi! Zaid broke my crayon!”
Farida looked up. Rafiq's fists were balled so tight his knuckles were white.
“Your hands are really squeezing. Are you angry?”
“Very angry!”
“That's a big feeling. Want to squeeze the stress ball or squash the playdough?”
“…Playdough.”
He grabbed the lump and squashed it flat. Then again.
“Better?”
“A little.” He opened his hands. “Can I have the tape to fix it?”
“Let's do it together.”

qa.q: What did Rafiq squash?
qa.a: The playdough.

qa.q: What do Rafiq's white knuckles suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: They show he was very angry that Zaid broke his crayon. The tight squeeze may also have been his way of holding back from hitting.

qa.q: What small step did Farida offer?
qa.a: She named the feeling and gave two safe choices, the stress ball or the playdough, to let the anger out.

qa.q: How might Zaid feel seeing Rafiq's fists?
qa.a: Zaid might feel scared of being hit, and relieved when Farida steered the anger into playdough.

grounding: A preschooler clenches his fists in anger, and his mother offers words for the feeling and a safe outlet.

passage:
Note by Raghav, playgroup leader, Friday.
We played musical chairs. When Eshaan was out, he stood by the wall with his fists clenched and his arms stiff. He didn't cry, but his face was red. I went over and said, “You wanted to win and you're cross.” He nodded hard. I gave him the squishy ball from our calm basket. He squeezed it until the game ended, then asked to help with the music. Next time I'll let the children who are out choose the song.

qa.q: What did Raghav give Eshaan from the calm basket?
qa.a: The squishy ball.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling as he stood by the wall with stiff arms?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated at being out of the game, and his red face suggests he may also have felt embarrassed.

qa.q: What does Raghav plan to change next time, and why?
qa.a: Raghav will let the children who are out choose the song, which gives them a job so being out feels less bad.

qa.q: How might the other children see Eshaan by the wall?
qa.a: They might not notice his clenched fists at all, since he didn't cry or shout.

grounding: The note shows a preschooler clenching his fists in anger and an adult giving words for the feeling and a safe outlet.

passage:
The kite was torn right down the middle. The neighbour's goat had trampled it in the field behind the house.

Anand stood over it, fists clenched so tight his knuckles went pale. His face turned red.

Anjali Didi knelt beside him. "You're so angry. You worked hard on that kite." She pulled a soft cloth ball from her pocket, the one they used for catch. "Squeeze this as hard as you want."

Anand squeezed and squeezed. Then he threw it at the fence. "Stupid goat!"

"Yes," Didi said. "Stupid goat. Tomorrow we'll make a new one."

qa.q: What had trampled the kite?
qa.a: The neighbour's goat.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when he clenched his fists?
qa.a: He was most likely angry and frustrated that his kite was ruined; his pale knuckles and red face show how strong it was. He may also have felt sad about the lost work.

qa.q: How did Anjali Didi help Anand with his anger?
qa.a: She named the feeling, gave him a soft ball to squeeze as a safe outlet, and offered a plan to make a new kite.

qa.q: If you were Anjali Didi, what would you want Anand to learn?
qa.a: That big angry feelings are allowed, and that there are safe ways to let them out, like squeezing a ball, instead of hitting.

grounding: It shows a preschooler clenching his fists in anger and an older sister offering words and a soft ball as a safe outlet.
